analysis.one_liner: Overhauls Medicare with HMO payment changes, patient protections, Medigap guaranteed issue, and new payment systems for home health and nursing homes.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan-styled Medicare overhaul with patient protections died in the Senate Finance Committee with zero cosponsors and no committee vote before the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would reshape Medicare around competition among private health plans: it changes how Medicare pays HMOs, guarantees that seniors losing plan coverage can buy supplemental (Medigap) insurance regardless of pre-existing conditions, bans 'gag clauses' that stop doctors from telling patients all their treatment options, and adds an ombudsman and quality 'report cards' for Medicare HMOs. It also moves home health and nursing home payments to fixed prospective rates, expands hospice care, adds Medicare fraud penalties, and promotes telemedicine for rural areas. Separately, it overrides state laws that regulate managed care or require certain insurance benefits.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries gain new protections: guaranteed Medigap eligibility after losing plan coverage, no pre-existing-condition exclusions during initial enrollment, a ban on HMO gag clauses, independent ombudsmen for grievances, faster appeals, emergency and dialysis access rules, unlimited hospice periods, and a respite benefit [S2][S3]. Medicare HMOs also gain: a payment floor of no less than 80% of the national average per-beneficiary cost, outlier payments, and preemption of state laws restricting managed care and state benefit mandates [S2][S3]. Frail elderly patients gain through permanent PACE and Social HMO program status [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Guarantees issue of Medigap policies without pre-existing-condition exclusions or health-based pricing to people who lose Medicare HMO or supplemental coverage for reasons like plan termination, insurer insolvency, or moving [S2][S3].

Prohibits HMO 'gag clauses' so doctors can openly discuss all treatment options with Medicare patients, and requires each Medicare HMO to designate an independent ombudsman to help members file grievances and appeals [S2][S3].

Requires quality 'report cards' and standardized comparative reports on Medicare plans, covering premiums, coverage, emergency care, prescription drugs, and disenrollment rates, to help beneficiaries choose [S2][S3].
Sets a payment floor so Medicare pays HMOs in all counties at least 80% of the national average per-beneficiary cost, gradually blending area and national rates [S2][S3].

Extends hospice benefits to unlimited 60-day periods, adds up to 32 hours of annual respite services, establishes permanent PACE provider status for community organizations serving frail elderly patients, and extends the six-month Medigap enrollment window to disabled beneficiaries [S2][S3].

Creates criminal penalties and property forfeiture for Medicare fraud, directs competitive bidding for durable medical equipment, and moves home health and nursing facility payments to prospective payment systems to slow spending growth [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Medigap insurers bear new rules barring health-based underwriting and pricing. Home health agencies and nursing facilities face prospective payment rates that cap their revenue per visit or per resident. Taxpayers absorb the HMO payment floor and outlier payments. Medicare HMOs face intermediate sanctions, quality standards, and ombudsman requirements. Patients in states with strong managed-care regulation lose those state protections because the bill preempts state benefit mandates and restrictions on utilization review [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Medigap insurers, home health and nursing home providers, taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The bill preempts state laws that mandate insurance benefits or restrict managed care, including laws regulating utilization review, stripping away state-level patient protections and leaving federal standards as the only backstop [S2][S3].

Its 'failsafe budget mechanism' automatically cuts Medicare payment rates across sectors like hospital, home health, and physician services whenever fee-for-service spending exceeds preset annual allotments, which could reduce payments that support patient care [S3].

Pushing more beneficiaries into HMOs and overriding state rules shifts care decisions toward private managed-care plans; the bill's own payments to those plans include outlier payments of up to 50% of costs above thresholds, adding federal spending [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The patient-protection half of the bill is real: guaranteed Medigap issue, gag-clause repeal, ombudsmen, and report cards address well-documented gaps for seniors navigating private Medicare plans. But the bill is a package deal — those protections come bundled with payment floors for HMOs, automatic across-the-board payment cuts if spending exceeds its own preset budget, and preemption of state consumer-protection laws. An honest reading is that it buys patient safeguards partly with state regulatory authority and with hard spending caps whose automatic cuts could hit care quality.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in March 1997 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Sen. Ron Wyden introduced the bill on March 3, 1997, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day [S5].
No cosponsors ever joined the bill [S4].

The only further actions were three sets of the sponsor's introductory remarks printed in the Congressional Record in March and April 1997; the Finance Committee never reported the bill and the full Senate never considered it [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo held: Medicare's existing HMO payment formula, Medigap underwriting practices, gag clauses, and state-by-state managed care rules all remained in place, so insurers and providers avoided both the new rules and the payment floors the bill would have created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo: existing insurers and providers

for.name: Ron Wyden
for.role: U.S. Senator from Oregon; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Medicare Modernization and Patient Protection Act of 1997 and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor three times in March and April 1997

against.name: Orrin Hatch
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Finance (105th Congress)
against.what_they_did: As Finance Committee chair, never scheduled the bill for committee consideration after its March 1997 referral; the committee took no action on it for the rest of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no other senator cosponsored the bill, so the partisan shape of support or opposition was never revealed on the record.

industries.note: The bill entrenches Medicare HMOs as the centerpiece of a choice-based Medicare — guaranteeing them a payment floor of at least 80% of the national average, outlier payments, and preemption of state laws restricting managed care — while imposing new quality standards, intermediate sanctions, ombudsmen, gag-clause bans, and report-card disclosure they must fund.

Guaranteed-issue and community-rating rules would bar Medigap insurers from denying coverage or pricing policies based on health status, medical history, or pre-existing conditions for people losing other coverage [S3].

A prospective payment system replaces cost-based reimbursement, capping revenue per visit and per episode but providing predictable payment and hearing rights before the Provider Reimbursement Review Board [S2][S3].
A per-diem prospective payment system with resident assessments and geographic ceilings replaces cost-based payment, with appeals available for decisions of $10,000 or more [S2][S3].
Extending hospice benefits to unlimited 60-day periods and allowing contracting with independent physician groups expands the potential hospice population [S2].

industries.industry: PACE and Social HMO community organizations
industries.note: Permanent PACE provider status and unlimited SHMO demonstrations would let nonprofit community organizations serve frail elderly patients under capitated Medicare and Medicaid payment [S2].
Competitive acquisition (bidding) for part B items would replace administratively set payments, squeezing suppliers in high-priced areas [S2].
